name: greek yogurt lemon pound cake
instructions:
Captured from a baking book (loaf cakes chapter, page 83 — author not identified in the excerpt). A greek yogurt pound cake — cold butter incorporated into the dry ingredients like pie dough, lemon-sugar-rub technique for citrus dispersion, cold-oven start for even golden exterior. Fluffier and more flavorful than [[french-yogurt-cake]] and stores well in the fridge — this is the cake to make in larger batches with fridge-friendly toppings.

MAKES ONE 9x5-INCH LOAF CAKE.

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- 4 oz (113g) COLD unsalted butter, cubed, + more for buttering the pan
- 1 cup (200g) granulated sugar, + more for coating the pan
- 4 tbsp (24g) grated LEMON ZEST
- 2 cups (250g) unbleached all-purpose flour
- 1 tsp (4g) baking powder
- 1/2 tsp (3g) baking soda
- 1/2 tsp (1.5g) Diamond Crystal kosher salt
- 2 large eggs (100g)
- 1 1/2 cups (360g) plain FULL-FAT GREEK YOGURT

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. PREPARE THE PAN: generously butter a 9x5-inch loaf pan and coat the inside with sugar.
2. MAKE LEMON SUGAR: combine the 1 cup granulated sugar with the lemon zest in a small bowl. Rub the zest into the sugar with your fingers until the sugar is bright yellow and fragrant.
3. In the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the paddle attachment, mix the flour, baking powder, baking soda, lemon sugar, and salt together — this disperses the soda and powder and breaks up sugar lumps. Add the cold butter and mix on low speed until the mixture resembles rustic sand, ~4 min.
4. Whisk the eggs and greek yogurt together in a small bowl. Slowly add to the butter-flour mixture on low speed. Mix until everything is combined and no dry flour remains.
5. Transfer batter to the prepared pan. Tap the pan on the counter a few times to burst air pockets.
6. COLD OVEN START: place the cake into a TOTALLY COLD oven on the center rack. THEN turn the oven on to 350°F (176°C). See notes on why this technique matters.
7. Bake until a toothpick or wooden skewer inserted in the center comes out with a few moist crumbs clinging (50 min to 1 hour). Cake will be tall, puffy, browned at the edges.
8. Cool in the pan for 30 min before removing. Cool completely before cutting.

Optional / welcome: almonds or walnuts folded in (see notes — nuts fine but optional).

KEEPS: well wrapped in plastic or in a sealed container for up to 1 week — this is a genuine make-ahead / large-batch dessert.
notes:
=== CHARACTER — FLUFFIER, MORE FLAVORFUL, FRIDGE-FRIENDLY (READ THIS FIRST) ===

This cake is FLUFFIER and MORE FLAVORFUL than [[french-yogurt-cake]] — despite the pound-cake format looking like it should be denser, in practice this reads softer and more cake-like than the french yogurt version (which is more bread-like / tea-cake in character).

More importantly for HOW to use it: this cake STORES WELL IN THE FRIDGE for up to a week. That storage capacity is what makes this the cake to reach for when you want to make a LARGER BATCH and eat over several days, and it's what supports pairing with FRIDGE-FRIENDLY TOPPINGS (ganache, buttercream, baker's frosting) that also last several days.

CONTRAST WITH [[french-yogurt-cake]]:
- FRENCH YOGURT CAKE: drier, breadier, less flavorful, dries out in the fridge → small batches (1-egg optimal), ephemeral toppings (compote, powdered sugar, whipped cream), eat same-day
- THIS CAKE (GREEK YOGURT POUND CAKE): fluffier, more flavorful, stores 1 week fridged → larger batches, fridge-friendly toppings (ganache, buttercream, baker's frosting), eat over multiple days

Different tools for different jobs. See [[french-yogurt-cake]] for the small-batch tea-cake side of this pair.

=== FRIDGE-FRIENDLY TOPPINGS — GANACHE, BUTTERCREAM, BAKER'S FROSTING ===

Because the cake keeps well fridged for a week, the right toppings are ones that ALSO keep well fridged for a week — they're the storage-life match. All of these work:
- CHOCOLATE GANACHE (dark or milk — dark is fine here, since the pound cake has enough body to hold up against it, unlike the french yogurt cake)
- BUTTERCREAM FROSTING (american or swiss — american buttercream especially since it's the most fridge-stable)
- BAKER'S FROSTING / other stable frostings — anything designed to hold shape and flavor over multiple fridged days

Ephemeral toppings (compote, powdered sugar, whipped cream) also work TASTE-wise, but they waste this cake's storage advantage — you'll eat the cake in one sitting to keep the topping fresh, and at that point you might as well have made a [[french-yogurt-cake]]. Match the topping's shelf life to the cake's.

=== NUTS ARE FINE BUT OPTIONAL (WALKED BACK FROM 'NO NUTS INSIDE') ===

Earlier notes here said 'no nuts inside — crumb can't suspend them.' Walked back. Nuts (almonds, walnuts) are FINE in this cake, like all cakes — the crumb is fluffy but not so delicate that nuts don't work.

That said, nuts are MORE OPTIONAL HERE than in [[french-yogurt-cake]]. This cake has enough flavor + moisture on its own; you're not depending on nuts to add character the way you might with the muted french-yogurt-cake base. Add them if you want extra texture and richness; skip if you want the pure lemon-yogurt register to lead.

=== FAILURE MODE — OVERPROCESSING / MELTING THE BUTTER (CRITICAL) ===

The other CRITICAL failure mode: OVERPROCESSING (or worst case MELTING) the cold butter during the mix. When butter overheats or over-integrates, it turns from solid fat coating flour particles into essentially OIL emulsified through the batter. Result:
- LESS RISE (the fat layers that were supposed to create air pockets are gone)
- BAD CRUMB (dense, greasy, no structural lift)
- FLAT, EGGY-TASTING FINISHED CAKE — same failure mode profile as UNDERCOOKING (see below). Two different causes, same result.

CAUSES:
- Stand mixer run too long or too fast on the cold-butter-into-flour step (past the ~4 min 'rustic sand' target)
- Butter that wasn't cold enough going in
- Warm hands / warm ambient kitchen when doing the mix
- Doing the mix in a metal bowl that pre-warms from the room

HAND-MASH ALTERNATIVE — BEURRE MANIÉ / PIE-CRUST TECHNIQUE IS OFTEN BETTER: instead of running the stand mixer, MASH THE COLD CUBED BUTTER INTO THE FLOUR + LEMON SUGAR + BAKING POWDER/SODA + SALT WITH YOUR HANDS or a fork/pastry cutter (like a pie crust or a beurre manié). Break the butter into pea-sized or smaller pieces coated in the dry ingredients. Stop as soon as the mixture looks like rustic sand — same target as the mixer method.

The hand approach gives you direct control over when to stop and doesn't risk the mechanical over-mixing / heat buildup that the stand mixer can cause. Especially useful if:
- Your kitchen is warm
- You're working with limited-strength cold butter
- You don't trust yourself to stop the mixer at exactly the right moment

Same result either way when done right; the hand-mash is a safer path for people who've had over-processed batches before.

Cross-reference [[russian-tea-cakes]] — same cold-butter-into-dry technique family; user's confirmed default there is the hand-mash pie-crust method for the same reason (control over stop point).

=== FAILURE MODE — UNDERCOOKING (BIGGEST TRAP) ===

The biggest failure mode with this cake is UNDERCOOKING. Easy to get timid when you see the exterior browning and think it's ready. IT WON'T BURN — keep going until the exterior is a SOLID DARK BROWN. Skewer-in-center-comes-out-with-a-few-moist-crumbs is the real signal; visible surface browning is not.

Cake will look done long before it actually is. The dense pound-cake crumb + greek yogurt moisture means the interior stays wet for much longer than the exterior color suggests. Pulling early leaves a dense, gummy middle. Pushing the bake longer gets you the tall/puffy/dark-golden loaf the recipe is going for.

Use a skewer or toothpick to verify — insert deep into the center. If it comes out wet, keep going. Add 5-10 min at a time and re-check.

=== ADD PARCHMENT PAPER TO THE EDGES (LOAF FORMAT) — HELPS PREVENT OVER-BROWNING WHILE THE MIDDLE COOKS ===

Because this cake needs a long bake to get the interior fully cooked (see UNDERCOOKING note above), the edges can push into over-browned territory before the middle catches up. LINING THE LOAF PAN WITH PARCHMENT PAPER (a strip that hangs over both long sides forming a sling) helps buffer the direct pan-to-cake heat transfer at the edges, giving you a more even bake with the interior fully done and the edges still golden rather than burnt.

Bonus: the parchment sling makes it easy to lift the cake out of the pan cleanly after cooling. Butter the pan first, THEN lay in the parchment sling on top of the butter — the butter helps the parchment stick to the pan and doesn't come out later.

=== COLD OVEN TECHNIQUE — WHY IT MATTERS ===

Source's technique: put the cake in a totally cold oven, close the door, THEN turn the oven on. The slow ramp-up as the oven preheats gives the cake time to set gradually rather than hitting a full 350°F all at once. Result per source: wonderfully even golden color on the outside, taller and puffier finished loaf.

Takes a little longer to bake (~50-60 min total from cold-start vs a shorter preheated-oven time). Plan for the extra time.

=== LEMON SUGAR RUB TECHNIQUE ===

Rub 4 tbsp grated lemon zest into 1 cup granulated sugar with your fingers until the sugar turns bright yellow and fragrant. This is a real technique step, not window-dressing — the sugar granules physically release the citrus oils from the zest through the abrasion, and the lemon-infused sugar then distributes through the entire cake. Skip the rub and just dump the zest into the batter and you get a less-cohesive lemon flavor.

=== COLD BUTTER, INCORPORATED LIKE PIE DOUGH ===

The cold butter goes in cubed and gets worked into the dry ingredients until the mixture looks like 'rustic sand.' This is closer to a pie-dough or scone technique than a cake technique — the fat coats the flour particles before liquid goes in, creating the pound cake's specific crumb (sturdy structure but tender bite) rather than the airy-fluffy crumb you'd get from creaming softened butter with sugar.

STAND MIXER OR HAND-MASH — HAND IS OFTEN SAFER: the source recipe calls for the stand mixer paddle attachment, ~4 min on low. Hand-mashing the cold cubed butter into the flour (like a beurre manié or pie crust — with your hands or a pastry cutter) is often a safer path — you get direct control over when to stop and avoid the mechanical over-processing / heat buildup that can melt the butter. See OVERPROCESSING failure mode above for why this matters. Cross-reference [[russian-tea-cakes]] which uses the same hand-mash pie-crust technique as its default.

=== HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM [[french-yogurt-cake]] (BRIEF) ===

The two cakes are close enough to confuse. Key structural differences beyond the character contrast above:

- YOGURT: greek (specifically — plain doesn't work here, needs the density) vs plain in the french yogurt cake
- FAT: cold cubed butter vs oil (with butter interleave) in the french yogurt cake
- LEAVENING: baking powder + baking soda (the soda reacts with greek yogurt's acidity) vs baking powder only in the french yogurt cake
- FORMAT: 9x5 loaf vs round (typically 9-inch)
- EGGS: 2 vs 3
- BAKE: cold oven start vs preheated 350°F
- LEMON: infused into sugar first (lemon-sugar rub) vs added as zest directly

Different recipes with different structural logic. Not interchangeable — reach for the one that matches your batch size, storage plan, and topping choice.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- [[french-yogurt-cake]]: the plain-yogurt round-cake sibling. Smaller batches, ephemeral toppings, tea-cake character. Different tool for a different job — see CHARACTER note above.
- chocolate-cake: Sally's triple chocolate cake (also uses buttermilk-or-yogurt). Different cake entirely; noted for completeness.
why_i_like_this_recipe: The fridge-friendly greek yogurt cake — fluffier and more flavorful than the plain-yogurt sibling, and stores well for a week so you can make a larger batch and top it with something durable (ganache, buttercream, baker's frosting) rather than an ephemeral topping. The cold-butter-into-dry and cold-oven-start techniques are worth knowing on their own; they show up in other pound cakes too.
